planting.note: Plant dormant canes in late winter to early spring; Cuthbert was the dominant US commercial red raspberry of the late 1800s and remains a vigorous heirloom choice for home gardens.

directions: Cuthbert is a nineteenth-century American heirloom red raspberry, selected near Great Neck, New York and sold commercially from the 1870s onward under the trade name Queen of the Market. Its vigorous floricanes produce a single concentrated midsummer crop of firm, deep-red conical berries that made it the backbone of the US commercial raspberry industry for decades before more disease-resistant modern cultivars took over. Give it full sun and well-drained, humus-rich soil, and support the canes on a wire trellis since older heirloom raspberries tend to lean heavily once loaded with fruit. Remove spent floricanes immediately after harvest and thin new primocanes each spring to maintain airflow, since Cuthbert has only moderate resistance to cane diseases compared with newer selections.

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in early spring; Herbert is an extremely cold-hardy Ontario heirloom raspberry long used as a breeding parent for hardiness and fruit size.

directions: Herbert is a nineteenth-century Canadian heirloom raspberry raised in Ontario and long valued in cold climates for producing some of the largest, juiciest berries of any raspberry grown at the time. The canes sucker aggressively and need a dedicated bed or annual root-pruning to keep the planting in bounds, but in exchange reward growers with outstanding winter hardiness well into zone 3. Because the berries are soft and fragile, they are best picked for immediate home use rather than shipping, and the plant served for decades as a parent in breeding programs seeking hardiness and fruit size. Plant in full sun with excellent drainage and mulch the root zone to buffer winter temperature swings.
sources: University of Guelph fruit breeding historical records

planting.note: Plant rooted tips or dormant stock in spring; Gregg was the leading commercial black raspberry of the late nineteenth-century Midwest.

directions: Gregg is a nineteenth-century heirloom black raspberry that became the leading commercial black cap variety across the American Midwest in the late 1800s, prized for its large, firm, richly flavored berries that held up well for market. Like other black raspberries, its arching canes root wherever the tips touch soil, so pin a few down each fall if you want extra plants, and otherwise tip-prune them back in midsummer to control spread. It is somewhat more sensitive to late spring frost at bloom time than some modern black raspberry releases, so a sheltered site helps protect the crop. Harvest is concentrated into two to three weeks in midsummer; remove spent canes right after the last picking to reduce carryover of cane blight and anthracnose.

planting.note: Plant root cuttings or dormant canes in spring; Kittatinny was discovered wild in New Jersey and became one of the most widely grown blackberries of the 1800s Northeast.

directions: Kittatinny is a nineteenth-century heirloom blackberry discovered growing wild along the Kittatinny Mountain ridge in New Jersey and introduced to cultivation around 1865, after which it quickly became one of the most widely grown blackberries in the northeastern and midwestern United States. The erect, thorny canes produce large, sweet, glossy black fruit that ripens over a fairly extended midsummer season, though the variety is markedly more susceptible to orange rust and winter cane injury than modern thornless selections. Grow it in full sun on well-drained soil and provide a simple two-wire trellis to support the heavy-fruited canes. Prune out spent floricanes after harvest and thin new canes in spring to improve airflow and reduce disease pressure.
sources: American Pomological Society historical variety records

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in spring; Lawton, discovered in New Rochelle, NY, was among the first blackberries deliberately brought into US cultivation in the 1850s.

directions: Lawton, also sold historically as the New Rochelle blackberry, was discovered growing wild in New Rochelle, New York, and promoted by William Lawton in the 1850s as one of the very first blackberries deliberately brought into cultivation in the United States. The tall, vigorous, thorny canes bear large, glossy fruit, though the berries must be left to fully darken and soften well past the point of looking ripe or the core stays hard and sour. It helped launch commercial blackberry growing in the Northeast before being largely superseded by hardier, less finicky varieties. Site it in full sun with good drainage, trellis the canes, and allow extra time between the berries turning black and actual picking to get full sweetness.
sources: American Pomological Society historical variety records

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in spring; Snyder, an 1850s Indiana heirloom, was famed for surviving Midwestern winters that killed less rugged blackberries.

directions: Snyder is an Indiana heirloom blackberry dating to the mid-1800s that earned a lasting reputation as the hardiest blackberry of its era, able to survive Midwestern winters that killed less rugged varieties outright. The fruit runs smaller and a touch more seedy than showier contemporaries, but the canes are extremely productive and reliable even on modest soils. It spread rapidly through farm windbreaks and homestead plantings across the Corn Belt because it needed so little coddling to produce a crop every year. Grow in full sun, trellis the upright canes loosely, and remove old floricanes after harvest; little else is required given the variety's famously tough constitution.

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in late winter to early spring; Malling Jewel was released by England's East Malling Research Station in the late 1950s and remained a UK garden staple for decades.

directions: Malling Jewel is a classic English raspberry released by East Malling Research Station in the late 1950s and grown in British gardens and smallholdings for generations afterward. It ripens its firm, richly flavored, dark red berries early in the summer raspberry season, just ahead of many later-season types, and the moderately vigorous canes are easier to keep in bounds than some older varieties. The plant is a dependable, relatively compact choice for home gardens, though it benefits from staking in windy sites since the fruiting laterals can be heavy for the cane. Prune out spent floricanes immediately after harvest and thin new canes each spring to around six per linear foot of row for the best fruit size.

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in spring in free-draining soil; Malling Delight, an early-1960s East Malling release, is prized for huge, well-flavored berries but is sensitive to root rot in wet ground.

directions: Malling Delight is an English raspberry from the East Malling breeding program, introduced in the early 1960s and still remembered among heritage-fruit growers for producing some of the largest, best-flavored berries of any raspberry from that era. It ripens over the early-to-midseason window with a concentrated, heavy crop on moderately vigorous floricanes. The main drawback that kept it from lasting as a major commercial variety is a marked sensitivity to root rot in heavy or poorly drained soils, so it performs best in raised beds or naturally free-draining ground. Mulch to conserve moisture without waterlogging the root zone, and remove spent canes promptly after harvest to limit disease carryover.

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in spring; Malahat was released by Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada's Agassiz, BC research station as an early-season raspberry for the Pacific Northwest.

directions: Malahat is an early-season red raspberry released by Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada's research station at Agassiz, British Columbia, part of a series of Pacific Northwest raspberry cultivars named for Vancouver Island and Fraser Valley place names. It produces its crop ahead of many standard midseason types, giving growers in the cool coastal Pacific Northwest an extended harvest window when paired with later cultivars. The vigorous floricanes perform best in the moderate, humid summers typical of coastal British Columbia and the maritime Pacific Northwest, and may need more disease vigilance in hotter, drier inland climates. Trellis the canes, remove spent wood after harvest, and thin suckers each spring to maintain good airflow through the row.
sources: Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada Pacific Agri-Food Research Centre

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in spring; Chemainus is a midseason raspberry from the same Agassiz, BC program that released Malahat.

directions: Chemainus is a midseason red raspberry from the same Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada breeding program at Agassiz, British Columbia, that produced Malahat and several other Vancouver Island-named raspberry releases. It fills the harvest gap between earlier and later-ripening cultivars, carrying firm, well-flavored berries on vigorous floricanes suited to the mild, damp climate of coastal British Columbia. Like its sibling releases from the program, it is best suited to cool-summer regions and may need extra attention to cane disease management in hotter climates. Provide full sun, a simple trellis, and prompt removal of spent floricanes after the harvest finishes.
sources: Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada Pacific Agri-Food Research Centre

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in spring; Qualicum is an early-season raspberry from the Agassiz, BC breeding program, named for the Vancouver Island community.

directions: Qualicum is an early-season red raspberry developed by the same Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada program at Agassiz, British Columbia, that released Malahat and Chemainus, and like them takes its name from a Vancouver Island community. It was bred to extend the early harvest window for Pacific Northwest growers, ripening firm, bright red berries on vigorous canes ahead of standard midseason varieties. The cultivar performs best under the cool, humid coastal conditions of its home region and is less commonly grown outside the Pacific Northwest. Stake or trellis the canes for support, and prune out fruited floricanes right after harvest to keep the planting vigorous.
sources: Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada Pacific Agri-Food Research Centre

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in spring and cut all canes to the ground each winter; Allgold is a golden-yellow autumn-fruiting sport of Autumn Bliss grown on primocanes.

directions: Allgold is a golden-yellow sport of the popular autumn-fruiting raspberry Autumn Bliss, discovered and introduced in England and valued for producing sweet, mild-flavored amber berries rather than the usual red. Because it fruits on the current season's primocanes, the simplest way to grow it is to mow or cut all canes to the ground each winter and let fresh canes crop from late summer into autumn. Its mild sweetness and striking color make it popular with children and for desserts where a less tart raspberry is wanted. Plant in full sun with rich, well-drained soil, and net the autumn crop if birds are a problem, since the pale fruit can be less obvious to pickers but is just as appealing to wildlife.
